event: Wednesday of week four: you wake at six, rested; you slept all night, the way you promised.
Bea is a warm weight at your back, still asleep, her blistered hand open on your hip.
You slide out, pull on a jumper and socks, and go down to the Thornfield kitchen in the half-dark.
You put the kettle on, and bread under the grill, and the window over the sink goes slowly grey.
At quarter past six the back door opens: Yusra, in from the infirmary, her coat damp with mist.
She has your flask in her hand. She stops in the doorway when she sees you, and stands there.
"You're up," she says. "I slept," you say. "All night. I said I would." Yusra almost smiles.
She puts the flask on the table. "It was still warm at two," she says. "Thank you, Nala."
She looks grey with tiredness, her eyes rimmed red, her hair coming loose from its knot.
You make her tea, sweet, and butter the toast, and put it in front of her; she sits, and lets you.
She eats one slice slowly. The kitchen is quiet but for the clock and the kettle cooling.
You sit across from her, and wait, and then you ask it: "What does the work keep in?"
Yusra puts her cup down very carefully, as if it might break, and looks at it for a long time.
"I had a girlfriend," she says. "Two years. Since my first year here. She's a doctor in Leeds."
"Junior doctor. We did the long distance thing. Trains on weekends. Letters. Phone on Sundays."
"In August she sent me a text." Yusra's voice stays level. "She'd met someone. On her rotation."
"A text," you say. Yusra nods. "Four lines. Two years, four lines. I've still got it. I read it."
"I haven't told anyone," she says. "Not my mum. Not my dad. Not anyone here. You're the first."
You reach across the table and take her hand, the one with the thin pink line across the palm.
She lets you. Her fingers are cold from the walk; you hold them in both of yours till they warm.
"I can't sleep," she says. "I lie there and I'm doing sums. Two years. What I missed. What I was."
"So I work. The infirmary. The library. Nobody asks a warden how she is." She stops. "You did."
You say she's allowed to be sad; you say two years is a lot to have taken off you by text.
One tear runs down her face; she lets it, which is somehow worse, and wipes it with her wrist.
"Pressure," you say softly, squeezing her hand. Yusra laughs, wet and surprised. "Good," she says.
She finishes the toast. Then she says, "I need to sleep," and stays sitting, and looks at you.
You walk her up the quiet stairs to the top floor, to room 1 at the head of them.
Her room is neat as a ward: a narrow bed, a desk of books, a jug and a glass, a lamp.
She sits on the bed in her clothes and takes off her shoes, slowly, like it's hard work.
"Will you sit," she says. "Just till I'm off. That's all." You sit on the chair by the bed.
She lies down on top of the blankets; you take the folded throw from the foot and cover her.
Her hand comes out from under it and finds yours, on the edge of the bed, and holds on.
"Lines," she says, eyes closed. "I know," you say. "I'm just sitting here." Her thumb moves once.
Her breathing slows. It takes ten minutes. Her hand goes loose in yours, and she's asleep.
You sit a while longer, watching her sleep, her face smooth and young without its guard on.
Then you lay her hand down on the blanket, and draw the curtain, and close her door very quietly.
Bea is up when you get back to 15, pulling on her tights. "Where've you been?" she asks.
You say Yusra came in off nights and you made her toast. Bea looks at your face a moment.
"Is she all right?" Bea asks. You say she will be, and that it's hers to tell. Bea nods.
She kisses you, quick and warm. "You're a good egg, Nala," she says, and goes off to row.
Morning: Sigils in the Drawing Room; you copy the wrong sigil twice, and Lin corrects it.
At lunch Kit sits down by you with a library book on wards; she's found an essay she likes.
"Grandmother says Penhallow wants what happened to you," Kit says. "So what happened to you?"
You think about room 1, and a cold hand warming. "Something," you say. "I'm still writing it."
Afternoon in the library: you write the essay properly, three pages, in one long go.
You write about a bandage, and a shell round a flame, and the hurt kept in while it mends.
You keep Yusra's name out of it, though she's in every line.
Lin reads it over your shoulder when you're done and says, "Oh," and goes back to her drawing.
At six you check room 1 on the way past; the door is shut, the curtain still drawn. Sleeping.
Dinner in the kitchen: Bea back from the boathouse, Priya and Amara cooking side by side again.
At half past seven Yusra comes down the stairs, hair washed, in a soft grey jumper, rested.
She stands in the doorway and finds you across the kitchen. "Nine hours," she says, only to you.
"Nine," you say. She nods, and takes a plate of dal from Priya, and sits down beside you.
Her shoulder rests against yours through dinner; when Bea passes the bread, Yusra passes it on.
After, she goes up first. At the turn of the stairs she looks back at you, and holds your eyes.
In 15 Bea's already in bed, rubbing cream into her blisters, a towel under her hands.
You get in beside her; she puts her chin on your shoulder and says, "You look happy. And sad."
You say both. Bea kisses your cheek and says that's allowed, and turns the lamp down.
You lie awake a little, thinking of a narrow bed in room 1, and hope she sleeps all night too.
A day at Hollowmere ends.
